fixes.explanation: That one is still about us, friend. The verse says love consists in this: not that we loved God, but that He loved us and sent His Son as the atoning sacrifice for our sins. The writer keeps his eyes on what God did. Even later he says, “We love because He first loved us.” (1 John 4:19)
Sins, friend. God sent His Son as the atoning sacrifice for our sins. The writer names the real problem out loud and then names what God did about it. I'd call that love with its sleeves rolled up.
Doubts is a natural guess, friend. But the text says God sent His Son as the atoning sacrifice for our sins. That's the word the writer chose, and it's the one that fits.

You got it, friend. No one has ever seen God, but the writer says that if we love one another, God remains in us, and His love is perfected in us. We can't see Him, yet love among us shows He's near. That's a mighty big thing to say about loving one another.
That's right, friend. The writer says, “By this we know that we remain in Him, and He in us: He has given us of His Spirit.” The proof isn't something we produce, it's something He gave.
Confidence, yes, friend. Love is perfected among us so that we may have confidence on the day of judgment. The writer says confidence, and that's the word to hold onto.

Yep, friend. The writer says, “…perfect love drives out fear…” Driven out, like a squatter getting the boot. When perfect love moves in, fear doesn't get a vote. That's the verb he picked, and I love it.
A trade sounds neighborly, but that's not how the verse puts it. The writer says, “…perfect love drives out fear…” The verse tells us what love does with fear: it drives it out.
Yes, a liar. The writer doesn't tiptoe, friend: “…but hates his brother, he is a liar.” That's a strong word. He's looking at what a person says next to how that person treats his brother.
A beginner sounds gentle, friend, but that's not the word he uses. The writer says, “…but hates his brother, he is a liar.” He doesn't soften it. The word is liar.
Stranger is a softer word than the one he picked. The writer says, “…but hates his brother, he is a liar.” He uses a plain, strong word and doesn't dress it up. Liar.

False is right, friend. The writer says, “For anyone who does not love his brother, whom he has seen, cannot love God, whom he has not seen.” The brother you can see, and the God you can't. And the writer says the one who doesn't love the brother he can see cannot love God.

A saying from Solomon is a fun guess, friend, but this letter doesn't mention him here. The writer says, “And we have this commandment from Him: Whoever loves God must love his brother as well.” It's a commandment from Him.
